Meqabyan (Ethiopian tradition) First Book of Meqabyan (Mäṣḥafä Mäqabyan I) (c. 600 AD)

Systematic exposition of resurrection through four natural parables — the MOST THEOLOGICALLY POLISHED chapter in 1 Mq. The argument proceeds through: (1) the vine and the tree (vv. 1-5), (2) the four elements gathered into the body (vv. 6-15), (3) day-and-night seasonal cycle (vv. 16-21), (4) the seed buried and rising (vv. 22-32). Per CROSS_REFERENCE_APPENDIX §10 the seed-buried argument (1 Mq 8:22-32) is the STRONGEST PAULINE PARALLEL in the entire trilogy to 1 Corinthians 15:36-38 ('that which thou sowest, thou sowest not that body that shall be, but bare grain... but God giveth it a body as it hath pleased him'). The four-element anthropology (earth + water + fire + wind) is the Empedoclean/Galenic Greek natural-philosophical anthropology mediated to Ethiopia via Syriac and Coptic patristic literature (parallel at 3 Mq 4:10 + 2 Mq 14:19).

Meqabyan (Ethiopian tradition) First Book of Meqabyan (Mäṣḥafä Mäqabyan I) (c. 600 AD)

'God waters its root from TWO BREASTS — FROM WATER AND FROM EARTH. But its wood he feeds from WIND AND FROM SUN' — the FOUR-ELEMENTS PARABLE for resurrection. Earth + water + fire(sun) + wind, the Empedoclean/Galenic anthropology mediated to Ethiopia via Syriac and Coptic patristic literature, applied as resurrection-analogy: as God reconstitutes the plant from elemental-sources, so He will reconstitute the body. Parallels 3 Mq 4:10 (Adam's-body composed of earth-water-fire-wind) + 2 Mq 14:19 (four-elements-resurrection-doctrine). The 'two breasts' (ሁለት ጡቶች) metaphor for the root-and-wood feeding-sources is distinctive Meqabyan-Geʽez vocabulary. Per CROSS_REFERENCE_APPENDIX Stage-3-broadening: the closest patristic parallels are Tertullian De Resurrectione Carnis §52 + Theophilus of Antioch Ad Autolycum 1.13 (the earliest extended Christian use of botanical/elemental-resurrection).

Meqabyan (Ethiopian tradition) First Book of Meqabyan (Mäṣḥafä Mäqabyan I) (c. 600 AD)

'And the WIND WHICH GOD CREATED gives fruit in their midst. So also is the resurrection of the dead' — closing the four-elements resurrection-parable with the wind-elemental as completion. The argument-from-tree-fruiting is paralleled in JOB 14:7-9 ('there is hope of a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again, and that the tender branch thereof will not cease... at the scent of water it will bud') + ECCLESIASTES 11:5-6 (the wind-and-growing-bones mystery — 'thou knowest not what is the way of the spirit, nor how the bones do grow in the womb of her that is with child'). Meqabyan unifies the elements-and-fruit pattern into a single direct-analogy: God-makes-the-tree-fruit, so God-raises-the-dead. The chapter's later seed-buried argument (8:22) is the COMPLETION of this elemental-analogy structure.
